one_liner: SMT-backed superoptimizer for LLVM IR that finds peephole rewrites stock LLVM misses; its published win is code size, not speed.
what_it_does: Souper harvests integer-typed expressions from LLVM IR, asks an SMT solver (Z3) whether a cheaper equivalent exists, and either prints the left-hand side with the synthesised replacement (the souper tool on a .bc file) or applies it automatically as an LLVM pass plugin registered at the peephole extension point. The sclang and sclang++ Perl wrappers drop into a build system as CC/CXX and add the plugin, a Redis query cache and per-query solver timeouts. It is mainly a tool for compiler developers: the README's RESULTS file and the paper describe LLVM commits and bug reports derived from its findings.
how_it_is_fast: It does not speed up code by itself; it finds missing peephole optimisations. Candidate expressions (plus path conditions and LLVM's known-bits and demanded-bits facts) are translated to SMT queries, and a synthesiser (enumerative synthesis or CEGIS, with optional Alive2 verification) searches for a shorter refinement; the pass then rewrites the IR and cleans up with DCE. Results are cached in RAM or Redis so repeated expressions skip the solver.
when_to_use: Compiler engineers hunting missed InstCombine-style rewrites in LLVM: harvest real code, let Souper propose shorter integer expressions, then implement the good ones by hand in LLVM.
Comparing LLVM's dataflow facts (known bits, demanded bits) against solver-derived ones; sclang exposes the harvesting switches.
Research on superoptimisation, where Souper is the reference baseline (Minotaur and the dataflow-pruning work build on it).
Experimental code-size reduction of a build already tied to LLVM 18 when a strong test suite can catch miscompiles.
when_not_to_use: Production builds aimed at runtime speed: the only published headline number is binary size, and the same paper reports (per search snippet) that the Souper-built Clang is about 2% slower.

Any toolchain other than its pinned patched LLVM (regehr/llvm-project branch disable-peepholes-llvmorg-18.1.6): GCC, MSVC and newer LLVM releases are unsupported and the repository was archived on 2025-10-30.

Floating-point or SIMD-heavy code: candidate harvesting skips every instruction whose type is not an integer (lib/Extractor/Candidates.cpp), so vector and FP code is untouched; Minotaur targets that gap.
Large builds without a Redis cache: each candidate costs SMT queries, and sclang sets a 15-second solver timeout per query.
Code where a UB-related miscompile is unacceptable: issue #311 (select turned into logic that introduces UB) has been open since 2018.

integration.form: LLVM pass plugin (libsouperPass.so) plus standalone tools (souper, sclang/sclang++ wrappers) built from source
integration.dependencies: patched LLVM/Clang 18.1.6 fork (regehr/llvm-project, branch disable-peepholes-llvmorg-18.1.6), KLEE fork (klee-for-souper-17-2), Alive2 fork (manasij7479, tag v7), Z3 4.13.0, hiredis (plus a Redis server for the external cache), zstd; build_deps.sh fetches and builds all of them
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (CMakeLists adds -std=c++20), CMake and Ninja; the README's GCC 4.9+ note predates that and is stale
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS hosts per the README; it rewrites target-independent LLVM IR, so output targets are whatever the bundled Clang supports
integration.thread_safety: not documented; Pass.cpp keeps the solver in a file-level global (std::unique_ptr<Solver> S), so it is built for one compile per process, which is how sclang uses it
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — sclang/sclang++ replace CC/CXX in a configure/make build, but only as wrappers around Souper's own patched Clang 18, and they need Z3 and (by default) a running Redis

gotchas: Known wrong-code and crash bugs were never fixed before archiving: #311 (Souper treats a select whose untaken arm has an undefined shift as a no-op, printing -128 where Clang and GCC print 0; Regehr called it likely a showstopper), #562 (a missing break in Pass.cpp getValue falls through to an out-of-bounds operand access), #166 (blockpc is unsound; blockpc exploitation is opt-in via SOUPER_EXPLOIT_BLOCKPCS). sclang ships a SOUPER_SKIP_FILES list 'for example because they trigger known bugs' and enables -souper-double-check by default.

Solver failures other than timeouts are printed as '[FIXME: Crash commented out] Unable to query solver' and skipped; the comment says this works around a protocol error seen once in SPEC 2017, so failed queries silently lose optimisations.
The Redis cache is unversioned: the README says to stop Redis and delete its dump file after every Souper upgrade, otherwise stale results from an older build can be reused.
The README's usage lines use the legacy pass manager ('-Xclang -load', 'opt -load ... -souper'); the current pass is a new-pass-manager plugin, and sclang passes both -Xclang -load and -fpass-plugin.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Souper over Minotaur when the target is scalar integer LLVM IR peepholes and you want the mature harvesting, caching and sclang build integration; Minotaur is its successor for SIMD/vector code and is the one with published runtime speedups. STOKE works on x86-64 assembly and K2 on BPF, so choose those for their respective targets.
verified_claims_summary: The only figure is from arXiv 1711.04422, seen through search snippets because arxiv.org and its mirrors are unreachable here: an automatic Souper pass produced a Clang 3.9 binary about 3 MB (4.4%, 64.3 versus 67.2 MB) smaller than the stock LLVM build. The same paper reportedly found that binary about 2% slower when compiling C++. No hardware, flags or SPEC runtime results were read, and the SPEC CPU 2017 figure in later work (2.32x) measures Souper's own speed after dataflow pruning, not faster output code.
status_note: Archived by Google on 2025-10-30 (last commit 2024-08-28) and pinned to a patched LLVM 18.1.6, with several wrong-code, crash and unsoundness issues left open (#311, #562, #166, #631); Apache-2.0 and usable as a research and LLVM-development tool, not as a production optimiser.
